cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on epsilon. This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from epsilon to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi define the exponential rates of bounded-width satisfiability and relate positive rate at width three to positive rates at other fixed widths. These are structural results about the hypothesis, not a proof of it.
The authors’ IPEC survey explicitly defines ETH by a positive infimum and distinguishes the number of variables from the complete input length.

The parameterized-algorithms textbook retains the positive-infimum definition, explains its distinction from ruling out a single subexponential algorithm, and gives consequences for parameterized complexity.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), c\ge 1\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on \(n\ge 3\) labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((2- \varepsilon )^{n}(n+\mathrm{L})^{c})\)?
cards.definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with \(w=B\lceil n+\log _{2}(\mathrm{L}+2)\rceil\) bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in \(n+\mathrm{L}\). The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants \(\varepsilon ,c,B\) and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

cards.title: Set Cover conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
cards.why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.

cards.definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.

The 2024 source studies reductions between such variants, but the card fixes the at-most-d covering version.

cards.title: FPT approximation of twin-width
cards.formal: Do there exist total computable functions \(f,g:N\to N\) and a constant \(c\ge 1\), and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer \(k\ge 0, A\) halts within \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations and either correctly reports \(tww(G)>k\) or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most \(g(k)\)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
cards.definitions: The input gives n, the \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of \(V(G)\), starting with the singleton partition and ending with \(\{V(G)\}\), each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair \(x\in X,y\in Y\) and a nonadjacent pair \(x' \in X,y' \in Y\) in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width \(tww(G)\) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the \(n- 1\) merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If \(tww(G)\le k\), rejection is forbidden. If \(tww(G)>k\), either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.

cards.title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
cards.formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.

cards.definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.

cards.definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.

cards.title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
cards.why: Deleting a small number of vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic model of repairing cyclic dependencies. Fixed-parameter algorithms make small deletion budgets tractable in principle, but the known factorial dependence is much larger than a fixed exponential base. The target asks whether directed cycle structure inherently causes that additional parameter cost.
cards.status_note: The checked 2025 primary papers retain the general single-exponential parameter question or the stronger unresolved subfactorial improvement. The SOSA 2025 bound retains k! and does not settle the target. Bounded subsequent-result checks through 2026-09-16 verified no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

cards.definitions: The input digraph is \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are not represented and have no effect. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\), \(t\ge1\), with arcs \((v_j,v_{j+1})\) for \(j<t\) and \((v_t,v_1)\). Thus self-loops are cycles of length one, and opposite arcs give a cycle of length two. For \(S\subseteq[n]\), the remaining graph is the induced digraph \(D[[n]\setminus S]\). A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\) for which this remaining digraph contains no directed cycle. Its cost is the cardinality \(|S|\); no vertex weights are present. There are no promises of planarity, bounded degree, bounded treewidth, a supplied solution or bounds on cycle length. Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all \(n,k,D\), no advice and no random bits. A valid input consists of the prefix \(1^n0\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, followed by exactly \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits encoding \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in most-significant-bit-first binary. The machine must halt and return the correct decision on every valid input. Each Turing-machine transition costs one step, including all input processing and preprocessing. No running-time condition on malformed strings is part of the target. The fixed encoding has length polynomial in \(n\), so ordinary polynomial-time changes of explicit graph encoding only alter the permitted polynomial factor. The quantified constants \(A,c,d\) are independent of \(n,k,D\). The target is worst-case exact decision, including NO instances; it requires neither an optimal deletion set nor enumeration of all solutions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the specified deterministic algorithm with its correctness and \(A2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) worst-case bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. A \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) algorithm, an exponent depending on \(k\) in the polynomial input-size factor, an approximation, or a result for restricted graph classes is insufficient for the affirmative answer. A lower bound conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis establishes only that conditional version of the negative statement.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 3.3 groups the general vertex-deletion and arc-deletion questions and separately asks about planar vertex deletion. The general unweighted vertex and arc versions have parameter-preserving polynomial reductions between them, so their single-exponential fixed-parameter existence questions are equivalent. Planarity is an additional restriction and is not presumed to be preserved by those general reductions.

The survey records the established \(k^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) parameterized running time and asks whether it can become \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\). Both are fixed-parameter bounds, but the exponent \(k\log k\) in the former is not bounded by a constant times \(k\).

The June 2025 Acta Informatica paper still calls improving the general \(2^{O(k\log k)}\) dependence to \(2^{o(k\log k)}\) a major open problem. Its positive results exploit additional graph structure, and bounds exponential in a treewidth or cycle-length parameter are not bounds exponential only in the deletion budget.

cards.definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.

context_blocks.title: A width that permits dense graphs
context_blocks.text: Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

context_blocks.title: Fixed thresholds versus the general optimization problem
context_blocks.text: Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound \(N^{k+2}\) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime \(f(k)N^{c}\) and c independent of k.

context_blocks.title: Approximate or supplied decompositions serve a different purpose

Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.

cards.title: Independent set algorithms from tropical circuit size
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) such that for every finite simple graph G on \(n\ge 1\) vertices and nonnegative integer weight vector w, A outputs the maximum independent-set weight within \(C(\tau (G)+n+\mathrm{L}+1)^{c}\) bit operations, where L is the total binary encoding length of w and \(\tau (G)\) is the minimum size of a tropical MWIS circuit defined below? Only G and w are supplied; neither \(\tau (G)\) nor a circuit is part of the input.
cards.definitions: G is given by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix. The n nonnegative weights are binary integers with delimiters, all counted in L. A vertex set I is independent when no edge has both endpoints in I. \(MWIS(G,w)=\max\)_{I independent}\(\sum_{v\in I}w_{v}\), allowing \(I=\varnothing\) with weight zero. A tropical circuit for G is a finite acyclic circuit with one designated output, arbitrary fan-out, input gates labeled \(x_{v}\) or the constant 0, and binary internal gates labeled max or + with their ordinary real-number meanings. No other constants or operations are allowed. Size counts every gate, including input and constant gates. An MWIS circuit must output \(MWIS(G,x)\) for every vector \(x\in R_{\ge}0^{n}\), so its topology depends only on G. Define \(\tau (G)\) as the minimum size of such a circuit. This minimum exists because finitely many independent sets can each be summed and their maximum computed. The output algorithm may use general deterministic computation, not only tropical operations. Constants C,c are uniform over all graphs and weight vectors.

cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
cards.formal: Do a computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\), an absolute constant c and a deterministic algorithm exist which decide isomorphism of graphs G,H in time \(f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^{c}\), where \(k=\max (\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H))\)?
cards.definitions: Graphs are finite simple undirected graphs given by adjacency matrices. Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency. For a graph G and \(X\subseteq V(G)\), the cut-rank is the rank over the two-element field of the adjacency submatrix with rows X and columns \(V(G)\setminus X\). A rank decomposition is a tree of maximum degree three whose leaves are bijectively labeled by \(V(G)\). Every tree edge partitions the leaves and hence defines a cut-rank; the decomposition width is the maximum of those ranks. Rank-width \(\operatorname{rw}(G)\) is the minimum width, with \(\operatorname{rw}(G)=0\) for at most one vertex. No decomposition or parameter value is supplied to the algorithm. The exponent c is independent of the rank-width.

cards.title: Polynomial exact metric sparsifiers with a crossing-edge budget
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that the following holds? For every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) of size r, and integer \(p\ge 0\), there is a set \(Z\subseteq E\) with |\(Z|\le C(1+p+r)^{c}\) having this universal property: for every finite nonempty label set D, every metric \(\mu :D\times D\to R_{\ge 0}\), and every terminal labeling \(\tau :T\to D\), if there exists a labeling \(\lambda :V\to D\) extending \(\tau\) with at most p crossing edges, then some labeling \(\lambda\)* of minimum \(\mu\)-cost among all such budget-feasible extensions has all its crossing edges in Z. The same Z must work simultaneously for every \(D,\mu ,\tau\) and depends only on G,T,p. This is the polynomial-size version of the contraction-based metric-sparsifier property in the source’s Theorem 22; that theorem’s earlier quasipolynomial upper-bound claim was later retracted.

cards.definitions: A crossing edge of \(\lambda\) is an edge uv with \(\lambda (u)\ne \lambda (v)\). Write \(X(\lambda )=\{uv\in E:\lambda (u)\ne \lambda (v)\}\) and \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mu}(\lambda )=\sum_{uv\in E}\mu (\lambda (u),\lambda (v))\). A metric has \(\mu (a,b)=\mu (b,a), \mu (a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and \(\mu (a,c)\le \mu (a,b)+\mu (b,c)\). The admissible labelings for a query are \(B(G,T,p,D,\tau )\)={\(\lambda :V\to D:\lambda |_{T}=\tau\) and |\(X(\lambda )|\le p\)}. If B is nonempty, the finite set \(D^{V}\) ensures that \(\min _{\lambda \in B}\operatorname{cost}_{\mu}(\lambda )\) is attained. The universal requirement is that this minimum equals the minimum with the additional constraint \(X(\lambda )\subseteq Z\); in particular the latter feasible set must be nonempty. The number p bounds crossings, not the real-valued metric cost. Labeling \(\tau\) need not be injective or surjective, and |D| is unbounded independently of \(p+r\). The constants C,c may not depend on the graph, budget, label set, metric or terminal labeling. Using \(1+p+r\) only handles zero parameters and is asymptotically equivalent to polynomial size in \(p+r\). Restricting all edges outside Z to have equal endpoint labels is exactly the labeling constraint imposed by contracting those edges; Z measures the original retained edges. The question is existence of this universal set, not the running time to find it, so it neither assumes rational metric entries nor a numerical oracle for them. Exact equality of optimum values is required; no multiplicative or additive error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal polynomial bound, or refute it by showing that no fixed constants C,c can bound the required retained edges over all G,T,p. A negative result must respect the quantifier order: every candidate small Z must fail for some label set, metric and terminal labeling with a feasible budgeted extension. Hardness of finding a small Z does not disprove its existence. Bounds for one fixed metric, a fixed number of labels, ordinary terminal cut values, or approximate values do not settle this target.

cards.title: Polynomial kernels for minor-free edge deletion
cards.formal: Does every fixed finite family \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple undirected graphs admit a deterministic polynomial kernel for \(\mathcal H\)-Minor-Free Edge Deletion, parameterized only by the number \(k\) of edges that may be deleted? An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\ge0\). It is a yes-instance if there exists \(F\subseteq E(G)\) with \(|F|\le k\) such that \(G-F\) contains no graph from \(\mathcal H\) as a minor. The kernel must return one equivalent instance of this same problem with total encoding length and output parameter bounded by a polynomial in \(k+1\), as specified below.
cards.why: A polynomial kernel would bound all information relevant to the deletion decision by a polynomial in the allowed number of changes, irrespective of the size of the original graph. This would make minor exclusion a broad source of effective preprocessing for edge repair. The distinction from vertex deletion matters because deleting a few edges can leave all vertices present and does not provide the same structural control as removing a small set of vertices.

cards.definitions: A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges; after contraction, loops are discarded and parallel edges are merged. These operations define containment only. In the deletion problem itself, the permitted modifications are deletions of original edges: \(G-F\) retains every vertex. A graph is \(\mathcal H\)-minor-free when no \(H\in\mathcal H\) is its minor. Families and their graphs may be disconnected; no member is required to be planar. The empty family and empty graphs are allowed under the stated minor definition, including their trivial cases. The family is fixed before the input graph and budget and is not counted as an input parameter. Graph \(G\) has labelled vertices \([n]\), possibly \(n=0\), and is encoded by a length-delimited binary integer \(n\) and its upper-triangular adjacency-bit array. The budget is a length-delimited binary integer \(k\); let \(L\) be the total input bit length. A polynomial kernel for fixed \(\mathcal H\) means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A_{\mathcal H}\), constants \(C_{\mathcal H}\ge1\), and integers \(b_{\mathcal H},d_{\mathcal H}\ge1\) such that for every \((G,k)\) it outputs a graph \(G^{\prime}\) and integer \(k^{\prime}\ge0\) in at most \(C_{\mathcal H}(L+2)^{b_{\mathcal H}}\) bit steps, with \[(G,k)\text{ is yes}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\text{ is yes},\qquad |\operatorname{enc}(G^{\prime},k^{\prime})|+k^{\prime}\le C_{\mathcal H}(k+1)^{d_{\mathcal H}}.\] The output uses the same graph and budget encoding and the same fixed forbidden family. The machine has a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet, with initially blank work tapes; input, output and all preprocessing are charged. No randomness, oracle, graph-dependent advice, extra weights or annotations, or calls to an instance-solving oracle are allowed. Constants and the finite program may depend on the entire fixed family, but not on \(G\) or \(k\); a uniform procedure compiling an arbitrary family into its kernel is not additionally required. Input graphs have no promise of being minor-free initially. The parameter bound includes \(k=0\) through \(k+1\). Binary encoding of very large budgets does not authorize time polynomial in their numerical value; the task has only \(|E(G)|\) possible edge deletions, so budgets above this value are equivalent to that capped budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universally quantified kernel-existence statement, or of its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite deterministic polynomial-time kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family, together with the equivalence and size/parameter bounds on every input. A negative proof must establish failure for at least one specified fixed family. A result for a family containing a planar graph alone, a vertex-deletion kernel, a kernel on already minor-free input graphs, a randomized compression, or a polynomial Turing kernel does not establish the full target. A kernel with output in a different annotated or weighted problem does not suffice unless the conversion to the stated unweighted problem and its size bound are proved. Conditional lower bounds remain conditional unless their additional assumptions are proved. This is a yes/no preprocessing question, not an estimate of the optimum deletion count.

cards.title: ETH barrier to single-exponential treewidth computation
cards.formal: Assuming the deterministic Exponential-Time Hypothesis (ETH) defined below, is an exact single-exponential parameterized algorithm for Treewidth impossible? Specifically, let \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) mean that there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), constants \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\) such that, for every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices and every integer \(0\le k<n\), \(A(G,k)\) decides whether \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le k\) correctly within \(C\,2^{ak}(n+2)^b\) steps. Under the assumption ETH, determine whether \(\neg\mathrm{FastTW}\) or \(\mathrm{FastTW}\) holds. This selects the explicit single-exponential example in the source’s broader request for lower bounds.
cards.why: Treewidth is a central measure of how close a graph is to a tree, and a decomposition is often the prerequisite for running efficient parameterized algorithms. cards.definitions: A tree decomposition of \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite nonempty tree \(T\) together with bags \(B_t\subseteq V\) for \(t\in V(T)\), such that every graph vertex belongs to some bag, every edge has both endpoints in one bag, and for each \(v\in V\) the set \(\{t:v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree. Its width is \(\max_t|B_t|-1\), and \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all decompositions. Graphs may be disconnected, with isolated vertices. Their input representation is the binary integer \(n\), the upper-triangular adjacency-bit array on labelled vertices \([n]\), and the binary integer \(k\), using length-delimited fields. The task is exact decision on every input, including graphs with treewidth larger than \(k\); there is no supplied decomposition or promise that the answer is yes. A Turing machine has a fixed finite number of tapes over a fixed finite alphabet, a read-only input tape, initially blank work tapes and a binary output. Each transition moves each head by at most one cell, and all input processing is charged. Programs and constants are uniform in both \(n\) and \(k\); no advice, randomness, oracle or unbounded-precision unit-cost operation is available. The single-exponential class here allows arbitrary constant polynomial factors in \(n\). ETH means that there exists a real \(\delta>0\) such that no deterministic machine in this model decides every 3-CNF formula \(F\) in time \(C\,2^{\delta N}(L+2)^b\) for any fixed \(C\ge1\) and integer \(b\ge1\). Here \(N\ge1\) is the number of Boolean variables, \(L\) is the full binary encoding length, and each clause is a disjunction of at most three literals, each literal being a variable or its negation. The input gives \(N\) in unary and the clauses as length-delimited lists of signed binary variable indices; repeated clauses are permitted. The treewidth and ETH time bounds are worst-case. Exponential dependence on the parameter alone is the target, distinct from an exponential dependence on the entire vertex count.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, with ETH as the explicit assumption, of either \(\neg\mathrm{FastTW}\) or \(\mathrm{FastTW}\). A proof of impossibility must rule out every constant \(a,b,C\) and every uniform machine meeting the full exact decision specification. A constructive answer must supply such a machine and prove the bound and correctness; an unconditional construction is sufficient for that direction. The accepted theorem must clearly retain its conditional scope and must not claim to establish ETH itself. Ruling out \(2^{o(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time does not rule out \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time. Approximate decompositions, algorithms assuming a decomposition is supplied, or bounds for another problem parameterized by treewidth do not meet this target. This is a binary complexity question, not a numerical approximation of the integer treewidth.

cards.definitions: A parameterized decision problem Q is a subset of \(\{0,1\}*\times N\), with input \((x,k), n=|x|\) and k supplied in binary. XNLP consists of those Q decided by one nondeterministic multitape Turing machine using time \(g(k)(n+2)^{a}\) and working space \(g(k)\log _{2}(n+2)\) for some total computable g and constant a, simultaneously on every branch. An input is accepted exactly when some branch accepts; all branches halt within the bound. The input tape is read-only and excluded from working space, which counts visited cells on the fixed finite-alphabet work tapes. A parameterized logspace reduction \(Q_{1}\le Q_{2}\) is a deterministic halting transducer mapping \((x,k)\) to \((y,k' )\), preserving the yes/no answer, with \(k' \le h(k)\) for a total computable h and space \(h(k)+C \log _{2}(n+2)\) for an absolute C. Its output is write-only and is not counted as working space. Q is XNLP-hard when every problem in XNLP has such a reduction to Q. In the conjectured forbidden deterministic algorithm there is no randomness, oracle or advice, and a single program handles all parameters. Constants, including c and the code computing f, are fixed for that program; f may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Using different computable functions in the time and space bounds is equivalent, since one common f can dominate both. Replacing n by \(n+2\) only handles short inputs. Slice-wise polynomial time allows its exponent to depend on k; the conjectured space bound permits dependence on k only in a multiplicative factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the simultaneous resource obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem, or refute it by an XNLP-hard problem and one uniform deterministic algorithm satisfying both bounds for explicit computable f and fixed c. A space bound achieved by a different algorithm, a time bound with a superpolynomial exponent in n at fixed k, or a result for only bounded parameter values does not meet the criterion.

cards.definitions: For a fixed graph H, an input to Independent Set on H-free graphs is a finite simple undirected graph G on n labeled vertices, encoded by its adjacency matrix, and a binary integer k with \(0\le k\le n\), under the promise that no subset of \(V(G)\) induces a graph isomorphic to H. The answer is YES exactly when there is a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|\ge k\) and no edge between distinct members of S. Only k is the parameter; H is fixed in the definition of the restricted problem and is not supplied as a variable-size input. Call H tractable if there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{H}, a\) total computable function \(f_{H}:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) and a constant \(c_{H}\ge 0\) such that \(A_{H}\) correctly decides every promised input in at most \(f_{H}(k)(n+1)^{c_{H}}\) bit operations. The algorithm is uniform over n,k and its guarantees are worst-case and exact. Behavior outside the H-free promise is unrestricted. Constants, algorithms and computable functions may depend on H, while \(c_{H}\) cannot depend on k or n. For \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) take disjoint copies of their vertex sets, preserve the edges within each copy, and put no edges between copies. Thus a graph contains an induced \(H_{1}\sqcup H_{2}\) precisely when it has disjoint induced copies of \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\) with no cross-edge between them. Excluding this one disconnected pattern is weaker than simultaneously excluding both \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\). The conjecture says that the set of tractable forbidden patterns is closed under ⊔. Its quantifier is over existence of algorithms for each fixed pair; it does not additionally demand one effective transformation that constructs an algorithm from descriptions of \(H_{1},H_{2}\) or from the two assumed algorithms. Input graphs G are not promised to be disconnected. Weighted Independent Set and randomized fixed-parameter algorithms define different variants; this card uses the source’s unqualified deterministic FPT convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \(H_{1},H_{2}\) satisfying the two tractability premises there exist an algorithm A, a computable f and a constant c, all allowed to depend on that pair, deciding the \((H_{1}\sqcup H_{2})\)-free problem in \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) time; or refute this universal implication. A refutation must establish both premises and failure of the conclusion for its pair. A \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof for the conclusion is only a conditional refutation unless the relevant FPT-versus-\(\mathrm{W}[1]\) separation is assumed explicitly. A result for the intersection of the two graph classes or for disjoint input components does not settle this statement.

cards.definitions:
A problem instance I has an explicitly represented finite universe U and a parameter k≥1. Its witnesses form a family W(I,k) of k-element subsets of U, not a family of ordered tuples or of certificates attached to the same subset. For example, when a witness is a k-vertex set supporting a path, several paths on that same vertex set do not create several witnesses. Each output is one subset, represented by its sorted list of element indices. The output order among subsets is unrestricted. Let N=|W(I,k)|; the algorithm is not given N. Instances with k>|U| have no witnesses.

“Self-contained” means that restricting the instance to X⊆U preserves exactly the witnesses contained in X: W(I|X,k)={W∈W(I,k):W⊆X}. The restriction examines only the retained elements and their relationships, is computable in polynomial time, and has encoded length polynomial in the original length L. A decision procedure on I|X therefore answers whether X contains a witness of the original instance. This is the inclusion query INC(I,X,k). Witnesses whose validity depends on their relationships to deleted elements, such as a vertex cover of the original graph, do not automatically satisfy this property.

The premise is a deterministic algorithm deciding whether W(I,k) is nonempty in time g(k)L^a, for some computable g and constant a independent of k and I. It thus also implements inclusion queries with an FPT bound. The desired enumerator may depend on the fixed witness problem, as may f and its constant polynomial exponent, but all of them must be uniform over its instances and parameter values. This is an implication between algorithmic existence statements; it does not additionally require an effective compiler from arbitrary decision-program code, or restrict the enumerator to a black-box oracle.

For a fixed input, let τ_i be the time when the ith distinct witness has finished being written, τ₀=0, and τ_{N+1} the termination time. Expected FPT delay requires E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤f(k)(L+1)^b for every i=0,…,N, with a constant b independent of k,I,i,N. When N=0 it bounds the whole time to termination. Expectation is over the internal randomness on this fixed input, without conditioning on a particular random execution history. The algorithm never outputs a false or duplicate witness and finishes the complete list with probability one. Its bound charges all work, including any preprocessing, inclusion-query execution, duplicate handling and writing outputs. The question imposes no additional polynomial-space requirement.

An expected-incremental-FPT bound instead allows E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤h(k)(L+i+1)^c, which grows with the number already output. An expected-output-FPT bound controls only the final expected time by h(k)(L+N+1)^c. Such a total bound may conceal a long wait before the next output. Dropping “expected” requires the corresponding deterministic bound. These notions are not identified with each other here. An extension query additionally asks whether some witness W satisfies Y⊆W⊆X for a prescribed Y; the premise provides no such forced-inclusion operation.

cards.definitions:
The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before inputs are supplied; it is not part of the parameterized input. Its members are finite nonempty undirected graphs and may be disconnected. The original source allows parallel edges, as in its two-vertex examples. Use finite undirected loopless multigraphs with all edge copies explicitly listed for the general convention here; simple graphs are included.

A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained from a subgraph by contracting edges. Contraction identifies their endpoints, removes resulting loops and retains parallel edges. It is not induced-subgraph containment or topological-minor containment.

The input consists of \(G\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It is a yes-instance if there is \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) contains no member of \(\mathcal F\) as a minor. All vertices have unit deletion cost. There is no planarity, degree, connectivity or sparsity promise on \(G\). The empty forbidden family is trivial and may be omitted. Since every forbidden graph is nonempty, \(k\geq |V(G)|\) is immediately a yes-instance.

A polynomial kernel is a deterministic algorithm that runs in a polynomial in the total binary input length and outputs a single pair \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) for the same fixed family. It must preserve the yes/no answer exactly on every input. There must be constants \(C_{\mathcal F},c_{\mathcal F}\) such that the total bit length of the output and the numerical value \(k'\) are at most \(C_{\mathcal F}(k+1)^{c_{\mathcal F}}\). Vertex labels can be renumbered. Counting only vertices while leaving arbitrarily many explicit parallel edges or a large encoded parameter would not suffice.

The algorithm, its polynomial running-time degree and the output exponent may depend on \(\mathcal F\). The question does not require one exponent that works for all families, nor an effective procedure constructing the kernel algorithm from an arbitrary family description. Such uniformity requirements would strengthen the target.

The parameter is the solution budget \(k\). It is not the size of a supplied vertex cover, a set whose removal leaves bounded treedepth, or another structural parameter. A kernel supplies one smaller equivalent instance, unlike an algorithm querying many small instances. Approximate kernels that lose a constant factor in deletion cost do not satisfy the exact equivalence requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family in this solution-budget model, allowing family-dependent exponents, or establish that some fixed family does not admit one. A conventional lower bound of the form “a polynomial kernel would imply NP is contained in coNP/poly” must retain that complexity assumption and is a conditional obstruction, not an unconditional separation. Special-family algorithms and approximate or structural-parameter kernels alone do not establish the universal claim.

cards.definitions:
A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has a finite explicitly listed vertex set and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc have no effect and need not be represented. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{0},\ldots,v_{r-1}\), with \(r\ge1\), having arcs from each vertex to the next, including from \(v_{r-1}\) to \(v_{0}\). Thus a self-loop is a cycle and two opposite arcs form a cycle.

A directed feedback vertex set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that the induced digraph \(D[V\setminus S]\) has no directed cycle. The decision instance is YES exactly when some such set has \(|S|\le k\). The remaining graph may be any directed acyclic graph, including a disconnected one.

Encode vertices by integers \(1,\ldots,n\), list all vertices and arcs, and encode \(k\) in binary using a fixed ordinary self-delimiting binary encoding. Measure preprocessing time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine in the total input length \(L\). The output uses the same encoding, with newly numbered vertices and a nonnegative binary integer \(k^{\prime}\). Bounding only the number of output vertices while permitting arbitrarily much auxiliary information would not meet the stated size requirement.

A kernel preserves the YES/NO answer, not necessarily the optimum value, the original vertex labels, or every solution. The output budget may differ from the input budget. The requirement is a single small instance of this same unweighted decision problem; a list of oracle queries or a compression into a different language is a different notion.

The preprocessing time must be polynomial in \(L\), uniformly for all \(k\). A procedure taking \(f(k)L^{d}\) time for an unrestricted computable function \(f\) is not by itself a polynomial-time kernelization. The case \(k=0\) is covered by the bound \(C(k+1)^{c}\). Allowing loops makes the model explicit and does not change the question: each loop forces its vertex into any deletion set, while repeated arcs can be removed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of an algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial preprocessing, exact answer equivalence, and polynomial output bit bound depending only on the original deletion budget, or refute that existence. A conditional lower bound must state its complexity assumption explicitly; it is not an unconditional refutation. A kernel using a larger structural parameter does not settle this target.
